confidence_note: Mouse study (100 days, 8-hour window, 28 percent lower weight) and eight-person pilot are from Salk/ScienceDaily reports of Panda's papers; the old text said 18 weeks and a 12-week human study, which could not be verified. Panda himself said human studies were needed, and Salk notes risk for undiagnosed fasting hypoglycemia, so a caveat is kept. Not checked against the book text itself.
facts: Panda's lab fed two groups of mice a diet with 60 percent of calories from fat. One ate whenever it liked; the other had access only in an 8-hour window each night, so it fasted about 16 hours a day.
Both high-fat groups ate the same number of calories.
After 100 days the mice that ate freely had gained weight and developed high cholesterol, high blood glucose, liver damage and worse motor control.
The restricted mice weighed 28 percent less and showed none of these effects, and did better on an exercise test.
Panda said at the time: we will have to wait for human studies to prove this. Co-author Megumi Hatori said there are bound to be limits.

A later pilot with eight overweight people who ate over 14 hours a day asked them to eat within 10 to 11 hours without changing anything else; after 16 weeks they had lost weight and said they felt more energetic and slept better.
Panda cautioned that eating duration is not the only way to improve health and may be risky for people with undiagnosed fasting hypoglycemia.
The pilot participants kept a weekly 'feedogram', a chart of their eating pattern, during the 16 weeks.
Two control groups of mice ate a standard diet with about 13 percent of calories from fat.
tension: Two groups ate the same calories of the same food; only the clock differed, and so did the outcome.
opening_idea: Start with two cages of mice eating the same high-fat food at different hours.

lessons.idea: The hours you eat may matter as well as how much; try narrowing them if your doctor agrees.
lessons.anchor: Mice with an 8-hour window weighed 28 percent less on the same calories.
lessons.example: Someone who snacks until midnight could set the kitchen closed at a fixed evening time for one week and see how they sleep.

reflect_final: If you wanted to test your own eating hours, what one change to the evening would you try and what would you check afterward?

use_cases.situation: A friend asks about eating windows.
use_cases.move: Say the mouse study found 28 percent less weight on equal calories, but humans are different; Panda said we must wait for human studies.

use_cases.situation: You want to try a shorter eating day.
use_cases.move: Tell your doctor first, especially if you have diabetes or low blood sugar, then try one week.

use_cases.situation: Your partner snacks late every night.
use_cases.move: Ask to compare how you both sleep this week if the kitchen closes at a fixed time.

pocket_idea: Same food, same calories, different clock: ask a doctor before you narrow your eating window.

conversation_variants.punchline_idea: Mice ate the same calories of the same food; the ones with an 8-hour window weighed 28 percent less.
conversation_variants.thirty_sec_idea: Panda's lab gave mice the same fatty food. Free eaters gained weight and developed liver damage; mice limited to 8 hours a night weighed 28 percent less. Panda said human studies were needed. A pilot with eight people eating within 10 to 11 hours reported better energy and sleep.
conversation_variants.question_idea: If you narrowed your eating hours, what would you want to notice?
